subtype: Approach: root cause analysis with the junior [Thinking]
passage: In a private cabin at a software firm in Gurgaon, Vinita closed the door and began with a question, not a verdict. "Tasks have been slipping for three weeks. What's making them hard?" Manav stared into his coffee. "I don't really understand the codebase," he said. "The payment module. I've read it three times. I didn't want to keep asking, everyone seems so busy." Vinita nodded slowly. If effort were the problem, she thought, he'd be hiding, not reading the same module three times. She had come ready to talk about effort. Instead she saw a gap in support: no walkthrough, and nobody to ask. "Thank you for telling me. Let's fix the explaining, not you." She booked an hour for a walkthrough the next day.

qa.q: Which module did Manav say he found hard to understand?
qa.a: Manav said he found the payment module hard to understand.

qa.q: Why did Manav avoid asking for help?
qa.a: Manav was afraid of bothering people, since everyone seemed so busy.

qa.q: What else could Vinita do to support Manav, and why?
qa.a: Vinita could ask a teammate to be available for quick questions each day, because a small regular source of help makes it easier to ask.

qa.q: How might Manav have felt when Vinita said to fix the explaining, not him?
qa.a: Manav probably felt relieved and less ashamed, since the problem was named as a lack of support rather than a fault in him.

grounding: Illustrates a lead asking a junior in private what is making tasks hard and finding the problem is missing support, not effort.

passage:
"Naveen, close the door for a minute. You're not in trouble."
Naveen sat down stiffly. "Is this about the payment module?"
"Partly," Aadhya said. "Your last three tasks came in late. I don't think you're lazy. I want to know what's making them hard."
He stared at his hands. "I don't want to sound stupid."
"You won't. Go on."
"I don't understand how the services connect. The codebase is huge. Everyone seems to just know it."
"Why didn't you ask?"
"You all looked so busy. I thought if I asked basic questions, you'd think I shouldn't be here."
Aadhya nodded slowly. So it wasn't effort. He'd been working late, trying to guess his way through it alone.
"Okay. That's a support problem, and that's on me too. Let's fix it together, starting tomorrow."

qa.q: What did Naveen say he didn't understand?
qa.a: He said he didn't understand how the services connect.

qa.q: What was Naveen afraid of, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was afraid of looking stupid and of people thinking he didn't belong; he sat stiffly, stared at his hands and said he didn't want to sound stupid.

qa.q: What else could Aadhya do starting tomorrow?
qa.a: Aadhya could pair Naveen with a friendly colleague and give him smaller tasks with short daily check-ins, so asking questions becomes normal.

qa.q: How does the private talk look from Aadhya's side?
qa.a: Aadhya realises the delays come from fear and missing support, not effort, and Aadhya takes some responsibility for not noticing sooner.

grounding: It shows a lead asking a junior privately what makes tasks hard and learning he doesn't understand the codebase and fears asking, so the problem is support.

subtype: Approach: root cause analysis with the junior [Thinking]
passage:
When Madhav's pull requests kept slipping last winter, my first thought was that he wasn't putting in the hours. But I'd seen his laptop light on at nine at night, so that couldn't be it.
I booked the small meeting room and asked him one question: "What's making these tasks hard?"
He took a long time to answer. Then it came out in a rush. He didn't understand how the old billing code worked. Nobody had shown him. And he was scared that asking would prove he wasn't good enough for the job.
I remember feeling a bit sick. I'd been judging his effort when he was working harder than anyone, just in the dark.
We made a plan that afternoon: a walk-through of the billing code on Monday, and a rule that any question is fine in our team chat.
Looking back, that one question saved a good developer.
— Uma

qa.q: What did Madhav say he didn't understand?
qa.a: How the old billing code worked.

qa.q: How did Uma feel on learning why Madhav's work was slipping?
qa.a: Uma felt a bit sick and guilty, realising the judgement about effort was wrong when Madhav had been working hard without support.

qa.q: Which other approach could Uma combine with the walk-through?
qa.a: Uma could pair Madhav with a friendly colleague twice a week, so learning team habits doesn't depend only on one session.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt after the talk?
qa.a: Madhav was probably relieved and less afraid, since the fear of asking was taken seriously and questions were made openly welcome.

grounding: It shows a lead asking a junior privately what makes tasks hard and finding he doesn't understand the code and fears asking, so the issue is support, not effort.
